newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh's forex market a one-way traffic.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh's forex market a one-way traffic.

text.p: Bangladesh's foreign exchange market is shackled by government restrictions and a lack of experience among local players, dealers said. Activity is dominated by one-way flows as domestic banks cling to a cautious approach.
"We either sell or buy. A two-way trading mentality has yet to develop in this moribund market," said a dealer with a foreign bank.
He added that the volume of trade remained low in interbank trading, due to the one-way mindset.
"The banks are not taking any risk. That's why there is no volatility in the market," the dealer noted.
"This is partly because of lack of knowledge," another foreign bank dealer said.
Officials with the state-owned commercial banks acknowledged their lack of ability to boost the foreign exchange market.

"Frankly speaking, we don't have expertise like the overseas banks in dealing on foreign exchange. We normally shun two-way quotations because there is a lot of risk. We are basically sellers," said one dealer with a major state-owned bank.
He noted that local banks were still learning about foreign exchange dealing. "The system was introduced only in 1995," he said.
Others observed there was little scope for a pick-up in volatility because of the limits set by central bank for buying and selling of the U.S. dollar, which is the intervention currency.
However, some players favoured the central bank band on taka trading against the dollar. "It's okay at this moment. If it is removed the initial shock will be much more than the benefit," one said.

The forward market is still in its infancy, according to market players. They believe forward trading has been stunted by restrictions on domestic bank borrowings, rendering the activity almost non-existent in the local arena. Spot trading dominates local bank activity.
"Borrowing of foreign exchange for only seven days (as allowed currently) is very short. But some banks do forward selling of dollar against usance bills (treasury bills)," according to a dealer.
However, foreign banks are providing forward rates to their customers, a service termed "very essential" by local dealers.
The country has already allowed partial convertibility of the taka but central bank officials said there is no possibility of making the currency fully convertible.
Market opinion has it that the forex market was still not mature enough to cope with free flotation of the local currency.
"Time is not ripe for that. There's still a lack of knowledge in treasury management," one dealer said.
